text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Opposition Social Democrat leader Oskar Lafontaine says there will not be another tax summit with government members soon. But he said there could be informal contacts on pension reform
- Czech President Vaclav Havel hails the German-Czech declaration as a historic chance for reconciliation in address in Bundestag lower house of parliament
- Rape in marriage will soon be outlawed after free vote in parliament shows support for the bill

- Economic affairs council of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats says coalition proposals for pension plans do not go far enough. It says pension levels would fall more quickly and that longer life expectancy should be taken into consideration
HANDELSBLATT
- Arms industry is on brink of a new order as German firms cooperate to build a new type of armoured car
- Opposition Social Democrats expect higher taxes from Finance Minister Theo Waigel in government tax reform
- East German miners protest against cutting schemes aimed at retraining redundant miners

- Czech President Vaclav Havel addresses German lower house after his country signed declaration with Germany this year. Havel says the two countries should use the historical chance for reconciliation
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG

- Urgent call to fight unemployment. German President Roman Herzog says politicians will have to do something and says citizens question whether politicians have the right to repeatedly delay necessary change
- Czech President Vaclav Havel called Europe a common home in his address to the German Bundestag lower house of parliament
- Asylum seekers are to receive less in social benefits
- Building companies leaves Transrapid consortium. Chief responsibility for project now mainly on shoulders of Deutsche Bahn and the state sector
DIE WELT
- Czech President Vaclav Havel address German lower house of parliament, saying two countries should use historic chance and hails reconciliation declaration signed earlier this year
- CDU parliamentary chief Wolfgang Schaeble wants change in tax reform timetable. He says the reform should come into force not in 1998 as planned but 1999
- Apparently majority support group bill on outlawing rape in marriage
- East German coal miners demand more money for re-training schemes
- Experts from German Economic Institute in Berlin say Bonn row over tax reform endangers the economy

- German find it hard to change. Internationally the failure of tax talks between Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government and opposition Social Democrats was seen as an inability of the government to push through much-needed reform
- German President Roman Herzog says ordinary citizens have no more understanding for Bonn ritual of delaying important reforms
